title: Meet the real-life Scottish surgeon who inspired Sherlock Holmes
gist: Interview with medical historian Lindsey Fitzharris about her biography Sleuth-Hound on Edinburgh surgeon Joseph Bell, the inspiration for Sherlock Holmes, framing his work with police surgeon Henry Duncan Littlejohn as the birth of forensic medicine in the courtroom. Little investment signal; Fitzharris closes with medical optimism (cancer vaccine on the horizon) and alarm at US backsliding on measles vaccination.

insights.claim: Lindsey Fitzharris argues Arthur Conan Doyle knew Joseph Bell only as a teacher, so he transposed Bell's single most recognizable trait, diagnosis by observation, onto Sherlock Holmes, omitting Bell's empathy and family life.
insights.so_what: Low direct investment relevance; illustrates how iconic IP is built from caricatured first impressions.
insights.quote: So he took the most recognizable flashy trait of Bell and transposed that onto Sherlock Holmes.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette

insights.claim: Fitzharris says no major commercial book on Joseph Bell existed before hers, with the main prior work a 1982 book by Ely Liebow, and that Bell's diary, locked away by the Bell family for over a century, recently became available.
insights.so_what: Newly available primary sources are what enabled the book.
insights.locator: One of the things that happened
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette

insights.claim: Joseph Bell worked officially with Edinburgh police surgeon Henry Duncan Littlejohn, a pioneer of fingerprinting and courtroom photography, on high-profile 19th-century Scottish cases, marking the moment medicine entered the courtroom.
insights.so_what: Historical context on the origins of forensic science.
insights.quote: It’s about the moment that medicine enters the courtroom for the first time.
insights.locator: But Bell was a lot more
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette

insights.claim: Fitzharris contends much early forensic science was built on the brutalized bodies of women who never received justice, citing the case of baby farmer Jessie King, who took fees and killed infants in an era without birth control or legal adoption.
insights.so_what: Social-history framing; no direct market signal.
insights.quote: a lot of early forensics was built on the brutalized bodies of women in particular
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette

insights.claim: Fitzharris calls the Victorian era 'the golden era of murdering' because poisons like opium were sold over the counter, were hard to detect, and forensic medicine was immature, as in the Eugene Chantrelle opium-poisoning case Bell and Littlejohn helped solve.
insights.so_what: Shows how detection technology and regulation of substances shape crime rates.
insights.quote: I call it the golden era of murdering
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette

insights.claim: Fitzharris, a cancer survivor, is optimistic medicine will make chemotherapy and radiation obsolete and says a cancer vaccine is on the horizon.
insights.so_what: Anecdotal optimism about oncology innovation, not a data-backed forecast.
insights.quote: I’m hoping that chemotherapy or radiation treatments will become obsolete. They’re brutal. And there’s a cancer vaccine on the horizon.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette

insights.claim: Fitzharris warns the US is going backwards on vaccines for preventable diseases like measles because of short public memory, noting people mistake her smallpox images for AI.
insights.so_what: Vaccine hesitancy is a public-health and vaccine-maker demand risk.
insights.quote: I put up pictures of smallpox on social media, and people think it’s AI.
insights.locator: I know. We have short memories.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
